overview: Trevaunance Cove is St Agnes' beach: a small bay of sand and shingle at the bottom of Trevaunance Coombe, the steep valley that drops from the village to the sea. A headland gives it some shelter from the west, but it's open to the north and north-east. A pub, beach shop, café and toilets are all within a minute or two of the sand, while the village centre is about a kilometre uphill on steep roads with no pavement.

The cove has a long history as a harbour. The Tonkin family tried to build one here from the 1630s, and storms kept wrecking their efforts; a version involving Henry Winstanley, the engineer of the first Eddystone Lighthouse, was destroyed in 1705. A later stone pier served the St Agnes mines through the 18th and 19th centuries, and at low tide you can still see the remains of the old breakwater on the western side of the beach.

Low tide also uncovers rocks and rock pools, and you can walk along the shore to Trevellas Porth. Keep a close eye on the tide if you do, because if you get caught out the only way back is a very steep climb to the coast path. The cliffs are a geological SSSI with mineral veins showing in the rock, and the cove sits in the St Agnes Mining District of the Cornish Mining World Heritage Site.

text: Spot guides describe St Agnes as a fairly exposed beach break over sand with rocks around it, mostly producing rights and usually at its best around mid tide. Winds from the south and south-south-east are offshore. It picks up both local windswell and longer-range groundswell, but summer is often flat, so autumn to spring is your best chance of good waves.

When it's working it gets crowded, so be patient and follow surf etiquette. Rocks are the main hazard, and local safety guides also list strong currents, which build when the swell is bigger. Lifeguards only cover the cove in summer, so check RNLI dates and the flags on arrival. Outside patrol times it's better suited to surfers who can read a small rocky cove.

cards.label: Level
cards.title: Improvers and above
cards.text: Small days can suit improvers. Bigger swells, rocks and currents make it one for confident surfers.

cards.label: Hazards
cards.title: Rocks, currents and tide
cards.text: Avoid the rocks at the edges, watch for currents in bigger swell, and don't get cut off walking to Trevellas Porth.

cards.label: Conditions
cards.title: Mid tide, southerly wind
cards.text: Usually best around mid tide with winds from the south or south-south-east. Often flat in summer.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Three small car parks
practical.text: There are two private car parks near the beach and a council car park further up the approach road, which has a very steep entrance. At busy times, park legally in St Agnes and walk down.

practical.label: Access
practical.title: Steep in every direction
practical.text: The road down to the cove is very steep, as is the slipway by the old harbour. The walk back up to the village is about a kilometre on steep lanes with no pavement.

practical.label: Facilities
practical.title: Pub, café and toilets
practical.text: Public toilets, a pub, a beach shop and a café are all a minute or two from the sand. Seats along the road give you somewhere to rest on the climb.

practical.label: Lifeguards
practical.title: Summer only
practical.text: The cove has RNLI lifeguards in summer. Check the RNLI website for this year's dates and follow the flags.

practical.label: Getting there
practical.title: A30, then the B3277
practical.text: Leave the A30 at Chiverton Cross and follow the B3277 for about four miles into St Agnes, then follow signs to the cove. There's no public transport to the cove itself, so bus users will need to walk down from the village.

faqs.q: Is there parking at Trevaunance Cove?
faqs.a: Yes, but not much. There are two private car parks near the beach and a council car park further up the hill. On busy days, park legally in St Agnes and walk down.

faqs.q: Can you walk from Trevaunance Cove to Trevellas Porth?
faqs.a: At low tide you can walk along the shore. Watch the tide carefully, because if you get cut off the way back is a very steep climb to the coast path.

faqs.q: When is the surf best at Trevaunance Cove?
faqs.a: Usually around mid tide, with a southerly or south-south-easterly wind. It's often flat in summer, so autumn to spring is more reliable.

faqs.q: Can dogs go on Trevaunance Cove?
faqs.a: The cove isn't listed in Cornwall Council's dog restrictions table. Other guides mention lead rules in summer, so check the signs when you arrive.
